title: Study: Batteries lose lithium to the current collector - electrive.com
content:
A research team from Ruhr-Universität Bochum, the Helmholtz Institute Ulm, and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) has experimentally confirmed a previously only suspected aging mechanism of lithium-metal batteries. According to their findings, lithium ions deposit in the copper current collector.
Atom probe tomography confirms: Lithium ions accumulate in the copper current collector.
Image: Prof. Dr. Tong Li
Using atom probe tomography, scientists have demonstrated that lithium ions penetrate and become permanently bound within the copper current collector during charging and discharging. This process has a detrimental effect: every loss of lithium reduces the available battery capacity and shortens the lifespan of a cell.
According to the researchers, this effect worsens with the number of charge cycles and also occurs in modern lithium-metal batteries. Their investigations revealed that lithium accumulates at grain boundaries and interfaces of the copper foil as early as the first charge and discharge cycle. After several cycles, the structure of the current collector changes: its surface becomes nanocrystalline and oxidises, creating additional defects. These defects bind further lithium and oxygen beneath the surface while simultaneously promoting the decomposition of the copper current collector.
The researchers’ method enables the three-dimensional visualisation of individual chemical elements with sub-nanometre resolution, allowing them to observe for the first time where lithium is deposited within the copper current collector. According to the study’s authors, these findings are particularly relevant for the development of future battery generations. Lithium-metal batteries and so-called anode-free (‘zero-excess’) batteries are considered promising candidates for achieving significantly higher energy densities than today’s lithium-ion batteries. However, it had previously been assumed that lithium does not interact, or only minimally interacts, with the copper current collector. The newly published results challenge this assumption and suggest that lithium loss to the current collector has been underestimated as a cause of capacity degradation in such cells.
These findings come at a time of intense investment in new battery technologies.
For instance, the Fraunhofer Research Production Battery Cell (FFB) in Münster is currently establishing a research infrastructure where companies can test new cell chemistries and production processes at gigawatt scale.
A deeper understanding of such ageing mechanisms is especially critical for future battery concepts like lithium-metal or anode-free batteries to transition high-performance and long-lasting cells into industrial production.
The research team from Ruhr-Universität Bochum, the Helmholtz Institute Ulm, and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) recently published their detailed findings in the journal
Advanced Energy Materials

title: Chinese integrators now hold 76% of global BESS market, analysis shows – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, News
Chinese integrators now hold 76% of global BESS market, analysis shows
–  July 24, 2026 12:49 pm BST
Eight of the top 10 integrators worldwide are now headquartered in China as the country continues its dominance of the international battery storage market, latest analysis has revealed.
Firms with roots in the Asian battery tiger nation captured 76% of global market share in 2025, according to energy data analytics firm Wood Mackenzie.
“China has expanded its global BESS footprint at remarkable speed,” Wood Mackenzie said in its 2026 ‘Global energy storage system integrator market share’ report, released on June 29.
Tesla and Sungrow retained the top two positions for the third consecutive year, while China’s BYD advanced five places to claim third.
Jiayue Zheng, senior research analyst, said: “The combined share of the top three integrators fell from 36% in 2024 to 30% in 2025, but this reflects rapid overall market growth and the rise of mid-tier vendors rather than any weakening at the top.”
Tesla retained its leadership in North America, supported by its lithium-based Megapack hardware platform, Autobidder software, and US-based manufacturing.
NextEra Energy entered the top three for the first time, benefiting from its position as a vertically integrated self-integrator insulated from tariff disruption.
Looking ahead, the US ‘One Big Beautiful Bill Act introduces Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) compliance thresholds for projects seeking to take advantage of the country’s 48E Investment Tax Credit, with provisions taking effect from this year.
Non-FEOC sourcing requirements start at 55% of project costs in 2026, rising to 75% by 2030, a trajectory that will significantly constrain the ability of Chinese manufacturers to supply into the US market, Wood Mackenzie said.
Meanwhile, Sungrow retained first place in Europe while BYD closed the gap from fifth to second and Huawei entered the top three.
Chinese vendors now occupy all three leading positions. The market is expanding beyond the UK, Germany, and Italy, with Bulgaria, Romania, Belgium, Spain, the Netherlands, and Greece forming a distinct second tier of growth markets.
China-based CRRC topped the regional ranking for the third consecutive year, followed by HyperStrong and Envision and China accounted for roughly 85% of the APAC market.
However, Wood Mackenzie said Southeast Asia emerged as a “meaningful growth frontier”, with the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia advancing regulatory and procurement frameworks. Australia remained the region’s most accessible market for non-Chinese integrators, given its stringent technical standards and lender preferences.
Chinese integrators have also extended their reach across the Middle East and Latin America.
The United Arab Emirates announced a 5.2GW solar project paired with 19GWh of storage, and Saudi Arabia’s two BESS tender rounds covered a combined 5GW/20GWh.
BYD and Sungrow together captured 87% of the regional market. In Latin America, Chile led with the most mature regulatory framework, as BYD’s total contracted volume with Grenergy reached 6.5GWh across all phases of the Oasis de Atacama project.
Zheng said competition in the global BESS integrator market is shifting from scale alone to a multi-dimensional set of capabilities. Policy compliance, grid-forming technology, software-driven revenue optimisation, and financing support are becoming decisive competitive variables.
“Integrators that can meet these demands across diverse regulatory environments will build the most durable market positions through the remainder of the decade.”

title: Delta launches Sweden Sungrow BESS in boost for Nordic power sector – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, News
Delta launches Sweden Sungrow BESS in boost for Nordic power sector
–  July 24, 2026 12:13 pm BST
Delta's Sungrow BESS project
Delta Capacity has announced commercial operation of a 70MW/160MWh Sungrow PowerTitan 2 BESS in Sweden — which the partners say marks the launch of the largest individual such project in the Nordics to date.
Swiss-based Delta said on July 20 the Ånge BESS will contribute to balancing Sweden’s power system while offering rapid response capabilities and capacity for both frequency regulation and arbitrage across the volatile Nordic power market.
Ånge is owned by a joint venture between Delta and sustainable investment fund WOOD & Company Renewables Sub-Fund — which has led the project from design to completion.
The project was acquired from Renewable Energy Systems in February 2025 and has taken 15 months from procurement through to commercial operation. Financial details were not disclosed.
Delta said Sweden’s battery storage market is expanding rapidly as the country’s energy transition accelerates. The regulatory framework has enabled battery storage to participate in balancing markets, turning it into a revenue-generating asset, according to industry data.
Sweden and Finland together installed more than 1GWh of new battery capacity last year, according to Solar Power Europe’s EU Battery Storage Market Review 2025.
Sungrow country manager for Sweden, Samer Nameer, said: “Ånge is a great example of how large-scale energy storage is built in practice. Our role is to be a long-term partner and contribute to expanding renewable energy capacity in Sweden.”
Delta CEO Patrik Hes said The Nordic energy transition is moving fast and requires infrastructure that keeps the same pace.
“Sweden has great renewable resources, but flexibility is missing and that is exactly what Ånge provides.”
As of December 2025, Sungrow has installed over 1,000GW of power electronic converters worldwide.
Delta already has nearly 800MWh under construction and targets the build-out, commissioning, and operation of more than 6GWh of flexible assets by 2030.

title: Battery projects ‘driving Australian power market’ – Batteries International
content:

Battery projects ‘driving Australian power market’
–  July 24, 2026 11:36 am BST
RWE's 8-hour BESS site in New South Wales
A record 9GW of new Australian generation and battery storage capacity reached full output in the last financial year, according to latest data.
Battery projects continued to dominate the connections pipeline, accounting for 52% of total capacity, and were also the fastest mover through the applications process, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) said in its latest quarterly ‘scorecard’ released on July 20.
The 9.1GW total was more than double the result achieved in 2025 for power generation and storage projects connecting to the National Electricity Market.
While AEMO’s scorecard reported new generation and storage projects from initial application through to full output for the quarter ending in June, it also marked the end of fiscal 2026, providing a snapshot of annual outcomes across the connections pipeline.
Solar and battery hybrid projects are an increasingly significant component of the development pipeline with 4.3GW of applications received during fiscal 2026.
In addition, 2.4GW of solar projects started or completed the process of adding a BESS, reflecting the industry’s growing interest in combining low-cost renewable generation with flexible storage, said AEMO group manager for onboarding and connections Margarida Pimentel.
The overall picture demonstrated strong end-to-end performance across the pipeline, including a new record of 5.2GW for wind project applications.
However, Pimentel said the scorecard highlighted growing challenges in the delivery pipeline, with only 6.4GW making it through to delivery.
“Design changes and equipment substitutions can require additional assessment and re-work, while the sale of projects, extended financing and commercial readiness activities are also contributing factors.”
Nevertheless, Pimentel said battery and solar technologies will play an important role in delivering the diverse mix of resources needed to support Australia’s energy transition.

title: Retired EV batteries power industrial sites
content:
Moment Energy, Rivian, and Redwood Materials have each cleared a different barrier standing between retired EV packs and commercial energy storage.
July 23, 2026
An EV battery recovery operation gets started at Redwood Materials
Redwood Materials
Rivian and Redwood deploy 10 MWh second-life battery system at Illinois manufacturing facility.
Moment Energy achieves first UL safety certification for repurposed EV battery management systems.
Second-life batteries retain over 80% capacity and suit stationary storage with gentler duty cycles.
Engineers design EV battery packs to last hundreds of thousands of miles, so many packs retain substantial charge capacity even after the vehicle itself reaches end of life. Combine that with the growing volume of retired EV batteries from a strong EV market, and there is a clear commercial case for repurposing those batteries for energy storage before recycling.
However, projects in this vein have long been mired in red tape. Second-life battery storage projects are regularly hindered by permitting delays, insurance obstacles, and the absence of recognized safety standards. Overcoming those obstacles requires real-world deployments that demonstrate performance at scale and the certification infrastructure to validate safety in industry-specific ways.
In this article, we’ll take a look at two recent developments that address both sides of that problem: a partnership between
Rivian and Redwood Materials
that has put second-life battery storage to work inside a U.S. automotive plant, and a safety certification milestone from
Moment Energy
that establishes a recognized regulatory foundation for broader commercial deployment.
Lithium-Ion Battery Circularity: Challenges and Opportunities
EV battery packs age primarily through charge-discharge cycling and thermal stress, not through the passage of time alone. According to the
American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE)
, EV batteries at the end of a vehicle's life typically retain more than 80% of their original capacity.
The reason that residual capacity transfers well to stationary applications lies in the difference in duty cycles. Vehicle propulsion demands high peak power during rapid load changes, which stresses cells aggressively. Stationary storage applications like peak demand management operate with shallower, more predictable charge-discharge cycles, which slow further degradation and extend a pack’s useful service life by many years.
Porsche has been repurposing used EV batteries to help power Its Liepzig plant since 2024. Credit: Porsche
However, capturing that extended service life requires assessment and management.
Because packs degrade non-uniformly across their cells and modules, repurposers need to test and grade each unit individually before reconfiguring it for stationary use. Automakers build battery management systems (BMS) to optimize propulsion performance, not stationary duty cycles, which means repurposers must either adapt the original OEM system or develop a new one suited to the stationary application.
In April, Rivian and Redwood Materials
a partnership to install second-life battery energy storage at Rivian’s manufacturing facility in Normal, Illinois. Claiming this project will be the first repurposed battery energy storage system deployed at a U.S. automotive manufacturer’s own plant, the companies will deploy more than 100 retired Rivian battery packs into a system that will initially deliver 10 MWh of dispatchable energy.
Rivian Repurposes EV Batteries for Scalable Energy Storage
Redwood's energy storage system. Credit: Redwood Materials
In practice, Redwood Materials plans to integrate the battery packs into a Redwood Energy system using the company’s Redwood Pack Manager technology, enabling Rivian’s plant to dispatch stored energy on-site. That capability means Rivian can draw on its second-life battery bank to offset peak-rate electricity purchases during high-demand periods rather than pulling additional load from the grid.
The companies also designed the Normal installation to scale as more retired Rivian packs become available. Both companies describe the project as a model for deploying battery capacity at other manufacturing facilities without waiting for new grid infrastructure.
Where the Rivian-Redwood deployment demonstrated what second-life storage can do at the operational level, Moment Energy addressed a separate obstacle that has long constrained commercial projects. Specifically, the company recently
that it had become the first company globally to achieve UL 60730-1 functional safety certification for a BMS designed specifically for repurposed EV batteries.
Ascend Elements Files Chapter 11 After Trump Administration Pulls $316M Grant
As a company that specializes in building and deploying commercial-scale energy storage systems, Moment Energy built its BMS for second-life batteries from the ground up rather than adapting an automotive original system. The company says its proprietary BMS proactively manages repurposed packs for performance and safety while respecting the intellectual property of its automotive partners, such as Mercedes-Benz Energy.
Moment Energy claims the combined certifications remove the insurance and permitting obstacles that have historically kept second-life battery projects out of populated areas. Looking forward, it plans to use that regulatory standing to expand energy storage deployments across North America.
Moment Energy’s announcement was followed by the news the company had completed Megafactory 1, which the company says is the largest EV battery repurposing facility in the world. The facility, which went online just six weeks after
the project was announced
, transforms retired EV batteries into cost-effective, rapidly deployable energy storage systems that support critical infrastructure, including data centers, hospitals, factories and microgrids. It’s expected to produce 1 GWh of battery energy storage systems by 2030.
The Rivian-Redwood deployment and Moment Energy’s certification milestone address two historical challenges in the second-life battery market: finding credible commercial applications and meeting safety and regulatory requirements. The fact that both developments landed within weeks of each other suggests a meaningful step forward for the viability of EV batteries for energy storage systems.
The open question facing the industry now is how quickly certification frameworks, project pipelines, and supply chains can align to meet the energy storage needs of the grid at large.

title: How PSM & Datavault are Securing the Mineral Supply Chain
content:
How PSM & Datavault are Securing the Mineral Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
Datavault and PSM have proposed a strategic partnership to help support the lifecycle management of strategic mineral supply chains
Datavault AI has proposed a strategic partnership with Patriot Strategic Metals to build a Strategic Materials Acquisition Platform.
The initiative centres on institutional digital infrastructure designed to support financing, tokenisation, settlement and lifecycle management of strategic mineral assets, with clear implications for how
critical minerals
move through global supply chains.
This strategic partnership brings together physical strategic assets and on our institutional grade cyber secure digital infrastructure.
Nathaniel T. Bradley, CEO of Datavault AI
Copper, lithium and cobalt are in
increasing demand
due to their use in AI infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing, defence, robotics and electrification. This demand growth places additional pressure on sourcing networks that are already exposed to geopolitical strain.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), critical minerals have emerged as a frontline issue in safeguarding global energy and economic security in a world of high geopolitical tensions. The agency notes that growing geopolitical tensions, marked by a series of export controls on key materials and technologies, have heightened supply risks.
According to the IEA, China accounted for around 60% of global mining output in 2024. China also dominates the midstream and downstream battery supply chains, holding shares of 80% or more in many key areas, according to the agency.
This concentration could mean that buyers of
critical minerals
face exposure to a narrow set of geographic and political risks. The proposed platform is intended to address this by supporting acquisition, storage, transportation, certification, insurance and distribution of eligible strategic minerals.
The proposed partnership is expected to combine Patriot Strategic Metals' integrated strategic metals platform with Datavault AI's real-world asset tokenisation technology, AI-enabled digital infrastructure, blockchain-based settlement capabilities and enterprise software.
Real-world asset (RWA) conversion turns physical or traditional financial assets into digital tokens, using blockchain technology similar to that behind cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin. In this case, it is proposed as a digital tracking system for
critical minerals
moving through the supply chain.
Patriot Strategic Metals' integrated metals platform includes mining interests, long-term offtake agreements, refining, strategic inventories, commodity trading and supply chain operations. An offtake agreement, in mining, is a contract between a resource producer and a buyer, where the buyer agrees in advance to purchase a specified volume of future mineral output.
John K. Park, Managing Member of Patriot Strategic Metals, says: "Our partnership with Datavault AI provides the technological foundation to modernise the financing and movement of critical minerals through RWA infrastructure, digital settlement and institutional trade finance."
The IEA says growing geopolitical tensions, marked by a series of export controls on key materials and technologies, have heightened supply risks
China accounted for around 60% of global mining output in 2024
PSM’s broader procurement platform includes an arranged revolving procurement facility of up to US$20bn
The companies state explicitly that the agreement covers offtake agreements alongside broader supply chain operations. This could mean the platform is designed to give chief procurement officers a tool for shoring up supply chain resilience in
critical minerals
amid instability.
The agreement is also intended to support acquisition, storage, transportation, certification, insurance and distribution of eligible strategic minerals. Each of these functions touches a distinct point in the physical movement of minerals from extraction through to industrial use.
Certification and insurance provisions could show an attempt to build verifiable, auditable trails for minerals as they pass between parties. This may matter to buyers in defence and semiconductor sectors, where provenance requirements are becoming more common.
Storage and transportation elements suggest the platform intends to track physical custody of minerals, not just financial ownership. Combined with tokenisation, this pairing of physical and digital record-keeping is central to the companies' stated aims.
The companies say the proposed partnership contemplates an initial Phase I platform development programme of up to US$700m. This sum is intended to support institutional trade finance, digital settlement, technology integration, compliance and platform deployment.
Within the Phase I framework, up to approximately US$62m is allocated for Datavault AI-related technology integration. Earlier this year, Datavault AI expanded its partnership with IBM and its watsonx platform, aimed at tokenising data at the point of creation and turning raw inputs into authenticated, tradable digital property in real time.
The partnership is also expected to support Patriot Strategic Metals' broader procurement platform, which includes an arranged revolving procurement facility of up to US$20bn. According to the companies, this ecosystem will function through the International Elements Exchange.
John adds: "Together, we are creating a scalable platform designed to strengthen resilient supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, defence, energy and advanced manufacturing while positioning the US as a leader in strategic metals infrastructure."
The companies say the proposed partnership is intended to create diversified recurring revenue opportunities through multiple institutional platform services. Datavault AI would participate in 25% of net distributable platform profits under the terms described.
While the arrangement is framed around reshaping minerals procurement, it also carries a direct commercial return for the technology provider through software transactions. This dual purpose, resilience infrastructure paired with profit share, runs through the companies' public statements on the deal.
According to Deloitte, companies can use gen AI to reimagine operations, making sourcing and procurement smarter and more proactive while setting new efficiency standards. The Datavault AI and Patriot Strategic Metals agreement could be read as an application of this thinking to the specific case of
critical mineral
supply chains.
Nathaniel T. Bradley, Chief Executive Officer of Datavault AI, says: "This strategic partnership brings together physical strategic assets and on our institutional grade cyber secure digital infrastructure. By combining PSM's critical minerals platform with Datavault AI's patented RWA technology, we are building a framework to modernise how strategic commodities are financed, settled and managed."

title: Examining the Hidden Fragilities in Auto Supply Chains
content:
Examining the Hidden Fragilities in Auto Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
A Moody's Analytics report examines where global auto supply chains are facing hidden fragilities and financial risk within their supplier network
Around the world, supply chain risk has become a given, rather than being seen as a single event. This is prevalent in the auto supply chain, an industry often reliant on just-in-time manufacturing.
Financial stress, compliance, materials shortages and
cyber issues
have all hit the sector in recent years, in part driven by geopolitical risks and global trends.
Moody's latest analysis explores a pattern of growing vulnerabilities across automotive suppliers, which then trickle into the wider supply chain.
Key findings
More than 1,100 suppliers are carrying high operational risk
6.4% of auto suppliers carry high risk
Approximately 85% of Japan's suppliers are low risk
More than 2,800 of China's supplier base are at low or medium risk
Over the last few years, supply chain disruption has been a constant. Since COVID-19 hit, delays and other events have occurred every few months, driven by trade tensions, inflation, materials shortages, climate change and volatility.
Supply chains around the world have been operating in a reactive state, forced to pullback on production capabilities or stop altogether. For auto supply chains, many of which operate in a made-to-order production line, a vulnerability from one supplier can halt production entirely.
Outside of supplier issues, cost pressures, cyber vulnerabilities and geopolitical risks are all colliding, causing vulnerabilities across automotive supply chains. Moody's research, from almost 18,000 automotive suppliers around the world, 1-in-16 are exposed to high operational risk. These issues are increased due to impact from the Iran conflict, oil-linked product prices and materials risks of those hard to substitute.
Critical raw materials
are also facing a surge in demand, with an inability to maintain a resilient production line. These materials are used in the energy transition – including EVs and wind turbines – as well as data centres, smartphones and more. Many of these are are hard-to-substitute, meaning vehicles cannot be manufactured if organisations cannot get access to the materials.
Supplier performance is a major signal for
supply chain risk
, so increased transparency and visibility is critical for automotive manufacturers aiming to avoid disruption.
"Anticipating and mitigating operational risks among key suppliers remains a critical challenge for manufacturing supply chains," explains Andrei Quinn-Barabanov, Supply Chain Industry Practice Lead at Moody's Analytics, to Supply Chain Digital.
"Moody’s analysis of financial health indicators identifies more than 1000
automotive companies
facing financial pressure. Financial stress can create challenges for workforce stability, including risks to employee retention, experience and training levels. While these pressures may contribute to operational disruption, many of the associated risk signals can be identified in advance, giving companies an opportunity to take proactive action.”
Exploring suppler risk by region, Moody's finds that Eastern Europe has the highest risk globally, in relativity to its supplier population. The European supplier ecosystem is vulnerable, due to its thinner margins and limitations to absorbing pressure.
Though North American suppliers currently appear operationally stable, Moody's finds that some suppliers are under strain, as demonstrated by their financial health indicators.
Anticipating and mitigating operational risks among key suppliers remains a critical challenge for manufacturing supply chains.
Andrei Quinn-Barabanov, Supply Chain Industry Practice Lead at Moody's Analytics
Moody's research suggest that vulnerabilities may be starting to arise across the global network – with possibilities of the vulnerabilities interacting with one another, making them worse.
Turkey, Russia and Ukraine are noted as being part of the
higher-risk environments
Risks in each country come from different root causes – though it may look financially stable, underlying trends are already threatening long-term
supply chain integrity
Though Japan has one of the lowest-risk supplier profiles, with 85% of its 712 suppliers at a low risk, its domestic environment may cause issues. Japan's domestic supply chain is at risk due to an aging population and a slow-growing home market. This means it is limited in facing external shocks and its future supply chains may be vulnerable.
Germany has a moderate risk-warning, despite 7% of suppliers being at high risk. This is caused by a deteriorating auto parts supplier market, with quality lessening and increasing numbers of mid-tier suppliers raising cash on the private market.
Ecuador's auto supply chain is vulnerable due to ongoing economic fragility. It has a 78% high-risk supplier concentration, with a heavy reliance on external financing. Colombia has a high-risk concentration of 18%, caused by budget deficits, limited flexibility and weak business investments.
Moody's research is working to help organisations identify and mitigate potential risks, exploring when they come from domestic or macroeconomic issues. By integrating risk indicators into their processes, using thorough onboarding systems, due diligence and ongoing monitoring, organisations can work to mitigate the impact of disruption.

title: How o9 and NVIDIA are Driving Faster Supply Chain Planning
content:
How o9 and NVIDIA are Driving Faster Supply Chain Planning
Prioritise Us
NVIDIA and o9 are partnering to introduce faster supply chain planning to operations, helping organisations become more resilient and efficient
o9 is collaborating with
to ensure faster solve times for its supply chain operations.
In today's complex world, solutions need to be fast and efficient at simplifying workflows, with agility when operating amid volatility.
What matters is how quickly the organisation can understand what changed and decide what to do next.
Ashwin Rao, Chief Technology Officer at o9
Around the world, o9 is using its Digital Brain platform to
drive enterprise planning
. To transform this workflow even more, it is collaborating with NVIDIA by applying NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated optimisation solver, NVIDIA cuOpt, on its platform.
When NVIDIA cuOpt is integrated into the o9 platform, as well as being run on the NVIDIA Blackwell computing infrastructure, the companies have found more than 10x faster solve times for large-scale supply chain challenges.
To test the efficiency of this collaboration, the trial was conducted on a supply chain planning dataset, made up of approximately 30 million variables, 15.7 million constraints and 94 million nonzeros.
This reflects the complexity and the scale of large-enterprise inventory optimisation and production planning workloads.
"Solve time directly limits how many scenarios a planning team can evaluate in a given planning window, especially for large-scale LP problems with tens of millions of variables and constraints," Ashwin Rao, Chief Technology Officer at o9, explains to Supply Chain Digital.
"But speed alone isn't the full story — a fast system can still recommend a replenishment quantity that violates a contractual minimum order, or mistake correlation for causation, if it lacks structured reasoning about how decisions connect across the business.
"That's why o9 pairs GPU-accelerated solve speed with a neurosymbolic architecture, where the "middle 80%" traces plans, forecasts and inventory positions to identify the actual cause behind a number, not just a fast answer. The result is optimisation that's both faster and more trustworthy for decisions with real financial consequences."
The trial demonstrated an optimisation solve in 57.4 seconds, meeting optimal solution status. A CPU-based LP solver required 661.7 seconds to solve the same problem – this reflects a 10x reduction in solve time. By reducing an almost-11-minute compute time to just under one minute shows the levels of efficiency that this partnership can introduce.
Despite this immense reduction of time-taken, the objective value remained within 0.008% of the CPU solver's optimal solution, demonstrating no sacrifice of solution quality. When a solution can operate more efficiently, with the same level of high quality, it drives cost savings and greater worker productivity.
"The world of optimisation is evolving rapidly, and our Digital Brain
platform for planning
and decision-making is built to evolve with it," says Chakri Gottemukkala, Co-Founder, CEO and Chairman at o9.
"Demonstrating a 10x-plus speedup on a real, 30-million variable supply chain LP—with best-in-class solution quality—is a meaningful proof point for what GPU-accelerated planning can deliver. Our architecture is uniquely positioned to allow o9 enterprise clients to immediately benefit from our collaboration with NVIDIA."
The planning dataset was made up of 30 million variables
The solution has demonstrated 10x faster optimisation
The trial has demonstrated an optimisation solve in 57.4 seconds
Optimisation in planning helps transform large enterprises, solving a range of issues that prevent them from meeting demand. The increase in planning agility also helps organisations avoid risk – teams can enact more scenario planning, respond to disruptions faster and be more resilient.
"Faster solves let planning teams iterate multiple times in a day instead of relying on overnight batch runs, meaning they can respond to disruptions as they emerge rather than waiting for the next scheduled cycle," adds Ashwin.
"While no system can reliably predict every black swan event like a port strike or geopolitical shock, what matters is how quickly the organisation can understand what changed and decide what to do next. In practice, this pairs neural AI interpreting incoming signals with a symbolic layer connecting them to the inventory, capacity and financial outcomes already modeled in the business.
"Speed, in other words, is what makes real-time disruption response possible, but it's the underlying reasoning architecture that makes the response trustworthy enough to act on."
The collaboration between o9 and NVIDIA is working to transform efficiency throughout organisations, making operations more time-efficient and cost-efficient. Through the
demand planning capabilities
that are being expanded on, organisations are also more resilient amid ongoing geopolitical turbulence.
Chief Technology Officer

title: Roland Berger: Are Europe's Defence Supply Chains Resilient?
content:
Roland Berger: Are Europe's Defence Supply Chains Resilient?
Prioritise Us
As demand for critical minerals increased, the aerospace and defence sector finds itself facing supply chain issues and concerns of vulnerabilities
In recent years,
critical raw materials
have been facing a significant boom in demand, driven by the energy transition, the rapidly growing number of data centres, the increase in AI availability and the ongoing demand for smartphones.
This is causing ongoing delays in materials sourcing and shortages across critical materials – a problem currently hitting the European aerospace and defence industry.
In a new report, Roland Berger explores how supply chain issues for necessary materials is causing vulnerabilities, and offers key governmental solutions.
Aerospace and defence supply chains are only as strong as their weakest link.
Rachel Hugo, Senior Partner at Roland Berger
In recent years, the raw materials market has seen a major boom. What was once seen as a steady resource has now started to undergo major pressure. Ongoing geopolitical developments have reshaped supply chains around the world, placing raw materials front and centre.
Now, a range of critical supply chains have revealed their structural dependencies on raw materials, particularly as western demand for electrification increases. The global need for clean energy has contributed towards western realisation of underinvestment in domestic capabilities.
With China holding a dominant position in the rare earth elements market – 60% of mining output and more than 90% of refining capabilities – the western has begun to consider its supply chain vulnerabilities.
Though each country has its own list of critical materials, built off demand and production capabilities, NATO has identified 12 critical raw materials which are a strategic necessity while also facing a
supply chain risk
. These are: titanium, aluminum, tungsten, platinum, cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite, beryllium, gallium, germanium, and key rare earth elements.
Meanwhile, the European Critical Raw Materials Act labels 35 materials as essential for supply chain resilience amid Europe's strategic autonomy.
"Critical raw materials have become one of the most significant risks facing aerospace and defence manufacturers. Demand is rising sharply, whilst supply remains highly concentrated and vulnerable to disruption," Rachel Hugo, Senior Partner at Roland Berger and co-author of the report, told Supply Chain Digital.
"Titanium and rare earth elements sit at the heart of every major platform – engines, airframes, radars, electric motors – so any upstream constraint has an immediate impact on production and capability delivery.
Aerospace and defence supply chains
are only as strong as their weakest link. Roland Berger’s latest report suggests a cumulative aerospace-grade titanium supply chain gap of around 100 kilotons could emerge over the next decade if production and recycling capacity doesn’t scale more quickly. Even relatively small shortages can have ripple effects across aircraft and engine and defence equipment programmes, making the avoidance of bottlenecks a strategic priority."
Though Europe assembles its
aerospace and defence components
, a significant portion of raw material upstream processing is concentrated in China and Russia. The report, therefore, argues that there are three key measures that can be taken to avoid supply shortage:
Governments and industries have been working to ensure supply chain resilience, forming new alliances with other nations or investing into domestic production capabilities. To do so efficiently, organisations need to identify their most critical materials and develop risk mitigation strategies which are specifically tailored to their needs.
The report states that OEMs are predominantly at risk if there are early stage disruptions in the supply chain.
"No single organisation can solve this alone. Building a resilient raw materials ecosystem requires coordinated investment across OEMs, suppliers and governments," explains Adam Healy, Partner at Roland Berger and co-author of the report.
Critical materials in Europe's aerospace and defence supply chains
China and Russia are responsible for approximately 50% of high-grade titanium sponge
There is an anticipated supply gap of titanium, reaching 100 kilotons in the next 10 years
and defence sector need to act in order to mitigate supply chain disruptions which are already threatening to impact operations. The strain on critical materials, however, reaches beyond just this industry. With demand coming from energy, smartphones, data centres and more, markets around the world are at risk of being impacted. As a result, there needs to be cross-industry collaboration in order to proactively ensure the availability of raw materials in the long-term.
"There is no single solution," Rachel warns. "Manufacturers need to understand where their biggest material dependencies lie and take a proactive approach to securing supply through strategic partnerships alongside alternative sourcing, recycling and investment in domestic capacity. Ultimately, building resilient supply chains requires coordinated action across industry and government to ensure critical materials remain available for generations to come."
There needs to be mass investment into
western production
to enable stronger upstream capabilities. Short-term investments – both time and money – will reap long-term benefits, and not just for the aerospace and defence sector.

title: Heineken Italia Boosts Water Resilience in Supply Chains
content:
Heineken Italia Boosts Water Resilience in Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
Brewer’s Valore Acqua project in Puglia aims to safeguard water, support farmers & strengthen beverage supply chains under rising climate pressures
Italy is facing growing water stress as climate change reduces freshwater availability and places greater pressure on businesses, agriculture and local communities.
In Puglia, one of the country’s hardest-hit regions, declining reservoir levels have highlighted the need for long-term water resilience strategies to protect both local livelihoods and national supply chains.
The European Commission (EC) states that Italy experienced 3,192 extreme weather events in 2022, underlining how climate volatility is now a structural risk to production networks.
Heineken Italia is responding with an initiative designed to protect local water resources while supporting agriculture and industrial output in its beverage value chain.
The project reflects a wider shift in procurement and manufacturing towards strengthening supply chains by
improving the sustainability
of the natural resources they depend on.
According to the EC, more than 40% of Italy’s public water supply is lost due to leaks in the system, which increases pressure on aquifers that underpin agricultural and food production.
Heineken Italia has partnered with the Regional Agency for Irrigation and Forestry Activities (ARIF) to launch the Valore Acqua project in Massafra, home to one of the brewer’s four Italian breweries and a key node in its national distribution network.
The initiative aims to reduce pressure on the Murgia aquifer, one of southern Italy’s most important freshwater reserves, by restoring existing water infrastructure and increasing the use of surface water for agriculture that feeds into beverage and
food supply chains
Key facts: Heineken's Supply chain
Italy experienced 3,192 extreme weather events in 2022, with droughts costing up to €9bn (US$10.3bn) annually.
More than 40% of Italy’s public water supply is lost through leaks, increasing pressure on key aquifers such as the Murgia aquifer.
Heineken Italia’s Valore Acqua project in Puglia will reactivate a 10,000m³ storage tank linked to the Bradano River and San Giuliano dam to support local agriculture.
The initiative is expected to deliver an annual water benefit of 318,000m³, strengthening resilience for farms that supply ingredients like barley.
Since 2010, Heineken Italia has reduced brewery water use per litre of beer by around 60%, from seven litres to 2.9 litres.
The project is set to reactivate an unused 10,000m³ storage tank connected to the Bradano River and the San Giuliano dam, improving regional water logistics and storage capacity that
support upstream farming
“For Heineken Italy, sustainability is a strategic lever that guides our way of doing business and creating long-term value,” says Alexander Koch, Chief Executive Officer of Heineken Italy.
“Protecting natural resources and water in particular, is a responsibility that goes beyond the confines of our breweries and requires an approach based on innovation, collaboration and a long-term vision.
“With the ‘Valore Acqua’ project, we want to help build greater resilience in the communities in which we operate and confirm our desire to generate a positive and shared impact on communities, the environment and the production system.”
Once operational, the system will distribute surface water to agricultural land in Contrada Borgo Perrone, reducing groundwater abstraction and helping safeguard the aquifer against further depletion and saline intrusion that can undermine crop reliability.
“Italy consumes a high amount of water, 25% above the EU average,” says the EC, highlighting the importance of efficient water management for supply chain stability.
Completion is expected during the first quarter of 2028 before testing and certification begin, giving local partners a clear timeline to plan for more resilient sourcing and production.
Agriculture represents the largest share of Heineken’s overall water footprint, making
resilient farming systems
essential for both environmental protection and business continuity across its global supply chain.
The additional water availability is expected to strengthen the resilience of local farms, improve irrigation reliability and reduce the risk of soil salinisation, all of which directly affect yields for key ingredients such as barley.
“Valore Acqua represents a concrete example of how collaboration between businesses and institutions can develop solutions capable of strengthening the water resilience of local areas,” says Leo Gasparri, Sustainability Manager of Heineken Italy.
“The goal of this initiative, which we developed together with ARIF, is to help increase the overall availability of water at the local level, thus generating a shared water benefit that involves communities, agriculture and ecosystems.
“We hope that this project will become a positive example in other Italian contexts called upon to address the challenges posed by climate change and the growing scarcity of water resources.”
These outcomes support not only farming communities but also the wider beverage supply chain by helping secure the production of key ingredients such as barley while reducing climate-related risks to agricultural output and procurement.
As droughts become more frequent across southern Europe, improving water efficiency within supply chains is becoming an increasingly important
sustainability priority for manufacturers
and retailers.
According to the EC, droughts can cost up to €9bn (US$10.3bn) annually, which can translate into significant disruption and cost volatility across European supply chains.
The project forms part of Heineken’s wider global water strategy, which focuses on reducing water use in production, restoring water resources in communities and improving water stewardship throughout its agricultural supply chain.
Since 2010, Heineken Italia has reduced the amount of water required to produce beer by 60%, lowering consumption from seven litres of water per litre of beer to 2.9 litres, which improves operational efficiency and resource productivity in its plants.
Water is an essential resource for people, the planet, agriculture and of course for our business.
Simon Henzell-Thomas, Global Sustainability Director, The Heineken Company
Globally, the company has strengthened its 2030 targets by aiming to reduce average water use to 2.6 hectolitres per hectolitre of beer produced worldwide and 2.4 hectolitres in water-stressed locations, aligning production practices with local watershed conditions.
Water scarcity affects 30% of Europeans and 20% of land each year, states the EC, increasing physical and regulatory risks for supply chains dependent on water-intensive agriculture and processing.
Heineken also plans to fully balance the water used in its products in water-stressed areas by returning 1.5 litres of water for every litre of beer produced through watershed restoration, irrigation improvements, wetland restoration and reforestation projects that benefit local catchments.
“Water is an essential resource for people, the planet, agriculture and of course for our business,” writes Simon Henzell-Thomas, Global Sustainability Director, The Heineken Company.
“Through the recovery of existing infrastructure and the enhancement of already available water resources, the project aims to replenish up to 318,000 m³ of water per year, benefiting local agriculture and the community.
“We know that water-related challenges can be tackled by building solid partnerships and working together with local stakeholders.
“Since 2010, Heineken Italy has reduced water consumption - per hectolitre of beer produced in our breweries - by around 60%.”
Alongside operational improvements, Heineken is targeting 100% sustainably sourced barley and hops by 2030 using the Sustainable Agriculture Initiative Platform’s Farm Sustainability Assessment, embedding responsible water management standards at farm level.
The programme encourages responsible water management across farms, reinforcing the
resilience of agricultural supply chains
while supporting broader biodiversity, soil health and climate adaptation goals that are increasingly important to supply chain leaders.

title: Solar generated more electricity than coal and wind in May – EIA data
content:
Michelle Lewis
| Jul 24 2026 - 8:41 am PT
In May alone, solar-generated electricity exceeded that of both coal and wind, according to new data just released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), and reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign.
Moreover, solar, wind, and battery storage are projected to add about 83.0 gigawatts (GW) of new generating capacity in the US by May 31, 2027, while total fossil fuel and nuclear power capacity will fall by almost 4.7 GW.
According to the EIA’s latest “Electric Power Monthly” report released July 23 (with data through May 31, 2026), electricity generated by renewables during the first five months of 2026 was 10.1% higher year over year. The growth was led by utility-scale (>1 megawatt) solar (up 21.6%), small-scale solar (<1 MW) (up 12.8%), hydropower (up 10.8%), and wind (up 4.8%).
The electrical output of the nation’s nuclear and natural gas plants grew much more slowly – 1.3% and 2.5%, respectively. Electricity produced by US coal facilities dropped by 10.9%.
The combination of wind and solar, including small-scale solar, accounted for over 22.2% of US electrical production.
During the first five months of this year, wind and solar combined produced 57% more electricity than US coal plants and 26% more than its nuclear reactors. In May 2026 alone, utility-scale and small-scale solar generated 47,147 GWh. Coal generated 45,119 GWh, while wind generated 41,157 GWh.
All renewables combined, including biomass and geothermal, accounted for 30.3% of total US electrical generation during the first five months of 2026 – up from 28.2% a year earlier.
Between June 1, 2025, and May 31, 2026, the installed capacity of utility-scale solar increased by 27,995.1 MW, while that of small-scale solar and wind grew by 6,664.3 MW and 10,252.6 MW, respectively. The combined capacity of all renewable energy sources, including hydropower, biomass, and geothermal, expanded by 44,711.8 MW.
In addition, utility-scale battery energy storage capacity increased by 16,551.8 MW.
Coal capacity fell by 2,235.6 MW, while nuclear capacity dropped by 27.6 MW. However, natural gas capacity rose by 6,289.0 MW.
As of May 31, 2026, renewable energy’s share of total US utility-scale generating capacity was 34.1%. EIA projects this to grow to 37.0% by May 31, 2027. Utility-scale solar will add 43,971.9 MW, expanding its share from 13.1% to 16.1%, while wind will grow by 9,414.4 MW (including 3,355.0 MW of offshore wind), increasing from 13.4% to 13.6%. The mix of other renewables (i.e., hydropower, biomass, and geothermal) will add 284.2 MW.
The combined net capacity growth of all utility-scale renewable energy sources for the 12-month period (53,666.0 MW) is 41% more year over year (38,047.5 MW).
Meanwhile, EIA projects no new nuclear generating capacity and a net decline of 4,685.0 MW in fossil fuel capacity.
EIA’s figures don’t include small-scale solar. The estimated capacity of small-scale solar systems grew by 6,664.3 MW over the last year, bringing the total to 62,088.6 MW. EIA does not provide a forecast of small-scale solar capacity growth over the next 12 months, but the SUN DAY Campaign is assuming it will roughly equal last year’s growth (an additional 6,000 MW or more).
If small-scale solar increases by approximately 6,000 MW by June 1, 2027, it will bring renewable energy’s installed capacity to about 542,096.3 MW. By comparison, natural gas’s generating capacity would total 514,845.1 MW.
Solar power’s share alone would be more than one-fifth (20.3%) of total US capacity.
EIA foresees battery energy storage adding another 23,241.1 MW by June 1, 2027 – an increase of almost 48%, bringing the total up to 72,002.0 MW.
Thus, the combination of utility-scale renewable energy sources and battery energy storage will provide 76,907.1 MW of new clean energy capacity by late spring 2027. With the inclusion of small-scale solar, that figure could rise to close to or above 83,000 MW.
“Notwithstanding all the roadblocks erected by the Trump Administration, the growth of solar, wind, and battery storage is actually accelerating,” noted the SUN DAY Campaign’s executive director, Ken Bossong, “proving once again that one cannot stop an idea whose time has come.”

title: Tesla quietly closes its secret ~$2 billion AI hardware deal
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 24 2026 - 8:39 am PT
Tesla has closed the mysterious ~$2 billion acquisition of an AI hardware company that it first hinted at in April — and it did so, again, without naming the target or issuing a press release.
The deal was confirmed in a single passage buried in Tesla’s Q2 2026 10-Q filing, which for the first time attached a final price: $1.95 billion, paid entirely in Tesla stock and equity awards.
According to the 10-Q, Tesla “acquired an AI hardware company in an asset acquisition for $1.95 billion in Tesla common stock and equity awards” during the second quarter.
Of that, $1.73 billion is contingent — “subject to certain service conditions and/or performance milestones dependent on the successful deployment of the company’s technology.” Only $222 million was allocated to an actual asset: “a patent and related developed technology intangible asset.”
In plain terms, Tesla assigned just $222 million of hard value to what it bought. The rest is stock tied to keeping the acquired team in place and hitting deployment targets — the hallmarks of an acqui-hire, not a conventional acquisition.
This is the same acquisition Tesla
quietly disclosed in its Q1 2026 filing
, which we covered at the time. Back then, Tesla said only that “in April 2026, the Company entered into an agreement to acquire an AI hardware company for up to $2.00 billion,” with roughly $1.8 billion subject to conditions.
The Q2 figures line up with that agreement now closing: “up to $2.00 billion” became a finalized $1.95 billion, and the ~$1.8 billion contingent portion was set at $1.73 billion. The April agreement was consummated in the second quarter.
Tesla still has not named the company. It has not described the technology, the team, or why it is worth up to $2 billion. Market speculation has centered on chip startup DensityAI, which was mostly formed out of Tesla’s former Dojo team, but Tesla has confirmed nothing.
The most striking detail is how Tesla is accounting for it. Because $1.73 billion of the consideration is tied to performance milestones, Tesla only records an expense as those milestones become likely to be met.
For Q2, it recorded nothing: “no stock-based compensation expense related to the performance-based awards was recognized as the performance conditions were determined to be improbable.”
That is Tesla’s own assessment — that the deployment milestones for the technology it just bought are, right now, “improbable” to be achieved. It is an unusual thing to disclose about a company you were willing to pay up to $2 billion for.
The acquisition is also part of a broader pattern of Tesla issuing stock at a rapid clip. Tesla’s share count rose by roughly 198 million shares in the first half of 2026 — issued for “equity incentive awards and acquisitions” — while stock-based compensation jumped to $2.18 billion, up about 80% year over year.
Tesla has called 2026 its biggest investment year ever, pouring capital into AI compute, its Austin semiconductor development fab, the SpaceX-linked
Terafab chip project
, and next-generation AI5 and AI6 chips. It is even positioning its energy-storage business as AI infrastructure — pitching Megapacks to smooth the volatile power draw of AI training runs (SpaceX bought $405 million of them in the first half of 2026) and floating “megapods” of Tesla chips at its Superchargers to tap the network’s power for distributed AI compute. An AI hardware acqui-hire fits that push — even if Tesla won’t say what it bought.
For the second quarter in a row, Tesla has disclosed a multi-billion-dollar transaction as a single vague sentence in an SEC filing — no press release, no name, no explanation. First a $2 billion SpaceX stake, now this ~$2 billion AI hardware acquisition. For a company that posts about every incremental robotaxi expansion on X, the silence around where billions of dollars in stock are going is conspicuous.
Tesla assigned just $222 million of real, recognized value to the assets — a patent and some developed technology — while dangling $1.73 billion in contingent stock that only pays out if the tech actually deploys. Then, in the same disclosure, it called those milestones “improbable.” That is a company hedging heavily on a bet it just made, and all but conceding it may not pan out.
None of this is illegal, and acqui-hiring a small AI hardware team for its talent and IP is a defensible move in the current AI arms race. But Tesla shareholders are diluting themselves by hundreds of millions of shares to fund deals they can’t see, evaluate, or even attach a name to. At some point, “trust us” stops being a strategy. Who did Tesla buy, and why is it worth up to $2 billion? Shareholders deserve an answer that isn’t buried in a 10-Q.

Kia’s bet on electrified vehicles is paying off. In the second quarter, the Korean automaker sold 110,000 pure electric vehicles, up 88% from the same period last year.

the second quarter
, an increase of 151% from the same period last year. Hybrid vehicles accounted for nearly 30% (29.6%) of Kia’s US sales.

With new EVs and hybrids launching in key markets over the next few months, Kia expects to sell more vehicles in the second half of 2026 than it did in the same period last year.

all-electric EV3 SUV

title: Kingbull Discover ST 2.0 review: A surprisingly capable fat tire e-bike that stops just short of ‘premium’
content:
| Jul 24 2026 - 6:53 am PT
One of the easiest ways to get my attention is to slap the word “premium” on an affordable e-bike. Sometimes it’s justified. Other times it’s… aspirational.
The latter is where the Kingbull Discover ST 2.0 lands.
, this step-through fat tire e-bike promises a lot on paper: a torque sensor, hydraulic disc brakes, UL-certified battery system, Samsung cells, a 750W Bafang rear hub motor, and a claimed 60-mile range. That’s a compelling spec sheet for the price, especially compared to the sea of cadence-sensor fat tire bikes still flooding Amazon.
After spending some time riding it, I’d say Kingbull got more right than wrong here. But I’d also say the “premium” label they put right in the product title oversells what is ultimately a competent, value-focused direct-to-consumer e-bike that is decent at getting the job done but doesn’t bring to the table premium features that we see on other,
more up-market
fat tire electric bicycles.
The good news is that’s perfectly okay, since the bike still fulfills the requirements for a decent everyday runabout.
The Discover ST 2.0 is an enjoyable bike to ride. The 750W Bafang motor delivers the kind of smooth, predictable acceleration I’ve come to expect from Bafang hub drives. It isn’t trying to yank your arms out of their sockets, but it has plenty of power for city riding, bike paths, and will be fine at climbing moderate hills.
Even more importantly, Kingbull paired it with a torque sensor instead of the cheaper cadence sensor found on many bikes in this price range. That makes a noticeable difference. Pedal assist feels much more natural, responding to how hard you’re pushing instead of simply whether the pedals are turning. It’s the kind of feature that makes the bike feel more refined, even if the rest of the package isn’t exactly luxury-grade.
The fat 26×4-inch tires deserve some credit, too. They’re one of those features that make almost every ride a little more enjoyable, as long as you’ve got the battery to power them (you won’t like them as much if you’re forced to pedal all that rubber around). They soak up road chatter, smooth out broken pavement, and give the bike enough confidence to wander onto gravel roads, grass, or light trails without a second thought. No, this isn’t a mountain bike, but it doesn’t pretend to be one either.
Speaking of comfort, the suspension fork does its job… within reason.
Kingbull advertises an 80 mm lockout suspension fork, and that’s exactly what you get: a basic coil spring fork. It’s not especially plush or sophisticated, but expecting air suspension at this price would be unrealistic. Between the fork and those giant tires, the ride stays comfortable enough for everyday riding, even if aggressive riders will quickly discover its limits.
You’re not going to do any crazy trail riding on this fork, and I do wonder about its longevity, but keep in mind that this a barely $1k fat tire e-bike, so you’re going to have expect some compromises.
Braking is another pleasant surprise. Hydraulic disc brakes have thankfully become more common on affordable e-bikes, and the Zoom two-piston brakes here provide solid stopping power with predictable modulation. I’d much rather see hydraulic brakes than flashy but unnecessary gadgets.
One thing I’m also happy to see is the emphasis on safety. Kingbull says the bike is UL 2849 certified and that the 720 Wh battery is UL 2271 certified (and built using Samsung cells). Battery safety has become
an increasingly important topic in the e-bike industry
, and seeing manufacturers pursue recognized safety certifications is something I’d always like to encourage.
There are, however, reminders throughout the bike that this isn’t actually premium, or perhaps it is in the way every brand of dog food is now labeled “ultra premium”.
Fit and finish are perfectly acceptable, but not exceptional. Some of the components feel like exactly what you’d expect on a $1,100 direct-to-consumer bike. The drivetrain is Shimano’s basic Altus seven-speed setup – nothing wrong with it but also nothing to swoon over. Cable routing is clean enough, though not especially polished, especially considering that all the extra handlebar-mounted boxes means more independent wires to manage (the lighting and horn controls are on a separate unit from the pedal assist selectors and on/off switch, for example). Nothing feels cheap enough to be concerning, but neither does anything make you stop and say, “Wow.” The display is actually quite vivid and easy to read though, so they scored a few points there. And the half-twist throttle also gets some love from me.
But back on the negative side, the bike is also fairly heavy at around 77 lbs (35 kg). That’s more or less normal for a fat tire e-bike with a large 48V 15Ah battery, but it’s something you’ll notice if you have to carry it upstairs or lift it onto a bike rack.
And then there’s the direct-to-consumer equation.
Buying online allows Kingbull to pack in a lot of hardware for the money, but it also means you’re largely your own bike shop. If something needs adjustment after shipping or requires warranty work later, you’ll either need some mechanical confidence or a friendly local bike shop willing to work on direct-sale brands. That’s not unique to Kingbull, but it’s part of the ownership experience that’s worth considering.
Overall, I think Kingbull found a reasonably sensible balance here.
Rather than chasing gimmicks or inflating motor power numbers into the thousands of watts, the company focused on basic features and parts that actually improve the riding experience: torque sensing, hydraulic brakes, decent battery components, and a comfortable ride.
Calling the Discover ST 2.0 “premium” feels like a marketing department getting a little carried away. But strip away the buzzword, and you’re left with something much more honest: a solid value-oriented fat tire e-bike.
At just over $1,100, I think the bike punches above its price in several important areas. The torque sensor alone gives it a more refined ride than many similarly priced competitors, and I’m always happy to see manufacturers investing in UL certification instead of cutting corners where it matters most.
Could the suspension be better? Sure. Could the overall fit and finish be more polished? Absolutely.
But then it wouldn’t cost $1,119.
If you’re looking for a recognizable legacy bike brand with on-call customer support and years of good reputation for strong customer service, this probably isn’t your bike. That’s what the biggest name companies are for. If you’re comfortable with knowing you and perhaps a few internet forums will handle most of your servicing, and you just want an enjoyable, capable fat tire commuter that gets the fundamentals right without emptying your wallet, the Discover ST 2.0 makes a surprisingly convincing case for itself.

title: NHTSA denies Tesla door-release defect petition, opens new door rules
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 24 2026 - 6:16 am PT
NHTSA has denied a petition asking it to open a defect investigation into the hidden manual door releases on the Tesla Model 3. But in the same decision, the agency agreed to start writing new door-safety rules for the entire auto industry.
The denial, published today, covers 179,031 model year 2022 Model 3 vehicles. NHTSA said it found exactly one complaint matching the petition’s allegation — and it came from the same owner who filed it.
The petition, filed November 7, 2025 by Tesla owner Kevin Clouse, argued that the Model 3’s “emergency egress controls for the mechanical door release are not readily accessible and clearly identifiable,” in violation of federal safety standard FMVSS 206.
That standard covers door locks, latches, and hinges meant to keep occupants from being ejected in a crash. The problem is what it doesn’t cover. As NHTSA put it, “no requirements exist in the standard that address the Petitioner’s concern regarding the labeling and location of a mechanical door release.” So there’s nothing on the books to enforce.
NHTSA also leaned on the complaint math. As of March 13, 2026, it found a single consumer complaint about a concealed or unlabeled manual release creating an entrapment risk, and that complaint traced back to Clouse’s own VIN. It described a front-impact crash in which the car lost power and the electric door mechanism stopped working. The agency noted the 2022 Model 3 owner’s manual includes an “In Case of Emergency” section with illustrations showing where the manual release is.
The conclusion: “NHTSA does not believe that the issues presented by the Petitioner indicate the likelihood of a safety related defect that would warrant a defect investigation, and the issue is best addressed through the rulemaking process.”
Here’s the part that matters more than the denial. A separate petition landed at NHTSA’s Office of Rulemaking on November 4, 2025, asking the agency to create a brand-new federal standard mandating “a robust and obvious door egress system in all motor vehicles.” NHTSA granted it. It will now commence a formal rulemaking on emergency door releases.
The agency also spelled out the risk in plain language: “A concealed or hard to locate door release could prevent an operator or occupant from exiting the vehicle in the event of an emergency, such as a crash or fire.”
That’s the same concern that’s been building around Tesla for a year. In September 2025, NHTSA
opened an investigation into Model Y door handles
after parents reported children getting trapped in the back seat when the 12-volt system died. Days later, Tesla said it was
redesigning its door handles
to combine the electronic and manual releases into one motion.
Then in December, NHTSA
opened a probe into the Model 3’s emergency door releases
, the same vehicles at the center of this petition, following reporting on fatal crashes where occupants couldn’t get out. Congress got involved in January,
introducing the SAFE Exit Act
and citing 15 deaths tied to door-handle access. And Tesla is
facing a string of fatal door-handle lawsuits
, even as it ships a mechanical fix on cars in China.
The two tracks do different things. A defect investigation could have forced a recall of specific Tesla vehicles on a timeline measured in months. Rulemaking sets a standard for every automaker, but it’s slow — federal safety rules routinely take years to write, and any final requirement would apply to future vehicles, not the millions of Teslas already on the road.
So Tesla owners driving today’s cars get a future industry standard, not a fix for their own doors.
Read the denial closely and it’s not the clean win for Tesla that the headline suggests. NHTSA denied the petition on a technicality, one complaint and no existing standard that covers labeling, while simultaneously agreeing that door egress is a real enough safety problem to justify writing a whole new federal rule. You don’t start rulemaking over a non-issue.
The one-complaint reasoning also deserves a hard look. NHTSA is treating this specific petition in isolation, but it already has an open Model 3 door-release probe and an open Model Y investigation running in parallel, plus a stack of lawsuits and a bill in Congress citing 15 deaths. The problem isn’t that only one person complained. It’s that Tesla built a car where the way out in an emergency depends on electricity, and buried the manual backup where panicked people and first responders can’t find it. That’s a design choice, and China already made Tesla fix it there.
The rulemaking is the right long-term move. But rules take years, and they don’t recall anything. Millions of Teslas with hard-to-find manual releases stay on the road in the meantime.
